params.question: A 28-year-old woman has a serum ferritin of 4 ng/mL. This low serum ferritin indicates depletion of iron stores located primarily in:

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Haemoglobin in RBCs belongs to the functional pool (~65% of body iron), not the storage pool. Serum ferritin does not measure functional haemoglobin iron.

Correct. Ferritin is stored primarily in hepatocytes (largest total store) and reticuloendothelial macrophages (mobilised fastest). A small amount leaks into plasma — this serum ferritin reflects those intracellular reserves.
Transferrin carries iron in the transport pool — only ~4 mg at any time. Serum ferritin and serum iron (transferrin-bound) are distinct tests measuring different pools.
Myoglobin (~300 mg) belongs to the functional pool and binds oxygen in muscle. It is not part of the storage pool and is not measured by serum ferritin.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the three iron pools: functional (haemoglobin, myoglobin, enzymes), storage (ferritin in hepatocytes and RE macrophages), and transport (transferrin). Serum ferritin reflects the storage pool.
Serum ferritin reflects intracellular storage iron — primarily in hepatocytes and macrophages — making it the first-line screening test for body iron reserves.

interactions.label: A 6-month-old infant exclusively breastfed since birth presents with microcytic

params.question: A 6-month-old infant exclusively breastfed since birth presents with microcytic hypochromic anaemia. The PRIMARY mechanism of iron deficiency in this infant is:

answers.text: Increased iron loss from occult gastrointestinal bleeding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Occult GI bleeding is associated with cow's milk, which causes microscopic mucosal injury — not breast milk. This falls in the increased-loss bucket, not the primary mechanism here.

answers.text: Decreased iron absorption due to an immature duodenal mucosa

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Iron absorption mechanisms are functional in healthy infants. The problem is insufficient dietary iron supply, not an absorptive defect.

answers.text: Insufficient iron intake — breast milk has low iron content

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Breast milk has low iron, and exclusively breastfed infants deplete their birth iron stores by approximately 6 months. Iron supplementation is recommended from 6 months of age.

answers.text: Increased iron demand from a concurrent systemic infection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Infection can cause functional iron trapping via hepcidin (anaemia of chronic disease mechanism), but the classic scenario of an exclusively breastfed infant points squarely to insufficient dietary intake.

overallFeedback.feedback: Think through the four mechanistic buckets — decreased intake, decreased absorption, increased loss, increased demand — and match each to the patient's demographics. For a breastfed 6-month-old, which bucket fits?
The four aetiological buckets of IDA are: decreased intake, decreased absorption, increased loss, and increased demand. In exclusively breastfed infants, decreased intake is the dominant mechanism.

interactions.label: Anaemia of chronic disease (ACD) typically presents as a microcytic hypochromic

params.question: Anaemia of chronic disease (ACD) typically presents as a microcytic hypochromic anaemia.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: ACD is typically normocytic, not microcytic. Although ACD is included in the TAILS mnemonic for microcytosis, this is because advanced, long-standing inflammation can eventually lower the MCV. The usual presentation remains normocytic normochromic.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. ACD is usually normocytic normochromic (MCV 80–95 fL). It appears in the TAILS mnemonic because prolonged, severe inflammation can eventually produce microcytosis — but this is not the typical presentation.

interactions.label: Two patients both have MCV 68 fL. Patient X has RDW 18% and RBC count 3.2 millio

params.question: Two patients both have MCV 68 fL. Patient X has RDW 18% and RBC count 3.2 million/µL. Patient Y has RDW 13% and RBC count 5.8 million/µL. The MOST likely diagnoses are:

answers.text: Patient X: IDA; Patient Y: beta-thalassaemia trait

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. IDA shows high RDW (anisocytosis from mixed-age RBCs) and low RBC count. Beta-thalassaemia trait shows normal RDW (uniform microcytosis) and a characteristically normal or elevated RBC count.

answers.text: Patient X: beta-thalassaemia trait; Patient Y: IDA

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is reversed. High RDW with low RBC count points to IDA (variable cell sizes, reduced production). Normal RDW with high RBC count is the hallmark of thalassaemia trait.

answers.text: Patient X: ACD; Patient Y: sideroblastic anaemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ACD is usually normocytic (MCV 80–95 fL), not 68 fL. Sideroblastic anaemia shows a dimorphic picture with very high RDW — neither pattern matches the clinical data presented.

answers.text: Both patients have IDA of different severity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: IDA at any severity does not produce a normal RDW with an elevated RBC count. Patient Y's pattern — normal RDW and high RBC count — is characteristic of thalassaemia trait, not severe IDA.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the comparison table: IDA causes anisocytosis (high RDW) with reduced RBC production, while beta-thalassaemia trait produces uniformly small cells (normal RDW) with an elevated RBC count.

RDW and RBC count are key discriminators: IDA = high RDW + low RBC count; thalassaemia trait = normal RDW + high RBC count. The Mentzer index (MCV ÷ RBC count) further supports this — >13 suggests IDA, <13 suggests thalassaemia trait.
